chapter: Joining and playing with Miles Davis
title: How Miles communicated sketches in the studio
summary: Miles brought scales, melodies and bass ostinatos, such as "It's About Time" and "Guinevere", but not whole pieces.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: If we could go back. That’s one of the reasons why I asked you how did Miles actually communicate that pattern to you. You said in Bitches Brew Miles would come in with some sketches. Now, how did he communicate those sketches? Were they written or did he sing them?
Yeah. Some of them were written. He had some scales, he also had melodies. One of the tunes… …on a later record, “Guinevere.” I think it was a Crosby, Stills and Nash song.

I think he might have had Wayne write a three-part harmony arrangement of that, so there were some written things and some bass ostinatos, but they were sketches. They weren’t whole pieces. For instance, “It’s About Time” [sings the melody] that was one sketch. Then it opens up in a B section the bass opens up [sings the bass line] so you got these two sections. A section, back to the B section, and that melody… when Miles passed away, we’ll get to that later. I wrote a piece for him called “Miles.”
